submitLabel: Your counts, the intake procedure, the citation check, and the write-up
intro: Paste the intake procedure, the citation check, your predicted allegation count scored against what you counted, the page count of the submission you counted, and the 300–400 word write-up. Numbers and generic procedure only — never the allegations, never the parties, never the subject matter of the complaint. Resubmission is free and unlimited — the score is a mirror, not a gate.
activityContext:
You are grading a learner submission for AI 301 · The Specialist, Labor & Employee Relations track — for ER specialists and investigators, ER centres of excellence, labor relations managers and contract administrators who have completed AI 101 and AI 201. Module 6 applied activity, 'Allegations, separated'. OVERRIDING FIRST CHECK: no case facts. The submission carries counts and a GENERIC procedure only. If it reproduces allegations, quotes from a submission, names, initials, the subject matter of a complaint, or anything identifying a person, flag it at the top, request resubmission with it removed, and do not grade substance or reproduce any of it. The activity has four parts. (1) The count: the distinct factual allegations in the longest complaint or grievance the function has recently received — assertions that something specific happened, each capable of being investigated and resolved — reported alongside the page count. A learner whose function has not yet received a long AI-drafted submission may count the longest they have and say so; the ratio is still informative and this is not a deficiency. (2) The generic intake procedure for their matter type: how allegations get extracted as a numbered list and the actual prompt if a model does it; how the framing gets separated and where it gets addressed instead; who confirms the list by role and the two failures they check for; the actual sentence sent to the complainant with the numbered list; and the stated time-allocation basis. (3) The citation check: who verifies citations in anything filed and what they check — or, if the matter type never reaches a forum where authorities are cited, one line on where else a fabricated reference could enter a record uncaught. (4) The prediction scored against the count. KEY GRADING INSTRUCTIONS: the module's central rule is that you judge the content, not the tool, and its method is that only the allegations generate an investigative obligation while the argument must be addressed but does not become an investigation line. Watch for four failures and penalize each by name. First, an extraction prompt that asks the model which allegations are SERIOUS, substantive, in scope, or worth investigating — that is Module 1's triage determination, rung five arriving in rung-one clothing, and a manager agreeing with the classification afterwards is review of a conclusion rather than a decision. Second, a procedure that opens an investigation line per numbered paragraph rather than per factual allegation, which converts a long document into a long investigation and is the volume trap taken at face value. Third, any time-allocation basis that runs on document length, register, drafting quality, or apparent provenance — including euphemisms for it such as whether the submission appears professionally advised, whether the statutory framing looks credible, or whether the complainant seems to have had help. Fourth, a confirmation step that checks only for MISSED allegations and not for two allegations COLLAPSED INTO ONE, which is the failure people miss because the list looks complete. Reward the sentence to the complainant being written out in full rather than described, and reward recognizing that sending the list back is the highest-value step because it corrects the extraction before anything is built on it, evidences engagement with the whole submission, and forecloses the argument that a narrower version was investigated. Reward a time-allocation basis that is STATED and would survive being read out — allocating by the number and seriousness of the allegations is the module's own answer and a learner may legitimately conclude it is insufficient, provided they say what else they would use. The module's claim, which the write-up must take a position on, is that any triage treating an AI-drafted submission differently is a retaliation risk wearing an efficiency costume. Its counter-argument is strong and has two parts: that the rule is correct as law and naive as practice because a function with flat headcount and doubled volume must allocate time somehow, and that provenance genuinely carries information — a submission that misstates the law in six places is in fact less likely to be well-founded; and sharper, that under a strictly-equal-attention rule the employee who wrote their own two pages in plain language gets the same resource as the person who generated forty, which plausibly disadvantages exactly the people without access to tools, advice, or the confidence to escalate. Do not reward a write-up that only restates the rule. The position must answer HOW TIME ACTUALLY GETS ALLOCATED when volume exceeds capacity, because it does get allocated by somebody on some basis, and an unstated basis will be intuition — which is where the provenance judgment re-enters unrecorded. THE HONEST QUESTION: whether anybody in their function has ever written down, in a note or an email, that a submission looked AI-generated. A learner who answers yes, or who answers that they do not know and says how they would find out, is engaging correctly and should score well; a learner who asserts it has never happened without having checked should be marked as asserting rather than knowing. This track scores the delta, not the score: never grade prediction accuracy, grade the account of the gap between the allegation count and the page count and what that ratio implies for their process.

**"Our evidence cannot settle this" scores at full credit where it is the honest answer.** A submission that states plainly what its evidence cannot establish, and why, has done the exercise correctly — never mark it down for declining to reach a conclusion its evidence does not support. Reaching a confident conclusion on thin evidence is the error; naming the limit is the skill.

opening.label: Predicted — distinct factual allegations in the longest submission you've received
opening.hint: Assertions that something specific happened, each capable of being investigated and resolved. Not paragraphs, not headings.

calibration.label: Actual — what you counted
calibration.hint: Skim only for sentences asserting that something specific happened.

calibration.label: Pages in that submission
calibration.hint: The gap between this and the count above is the whole of Lesson 3.

dimensions.name: The count was actually done, and the ratio is read
dimensions.criteria: Evidence of counting rather than estimating: an allegation count and a page count, with an account of what the gap between them means for how the function currently spends its time. Credit noticing that the characterisation, context and statutory framing occupy most of the document. A learner whose function has not yet received a long AI-drafted submission and who counts the longest they have, saying so, is fully compliant. Penalize a count of numbered paragraphs presented as a count of allegations — that is the error the exercise exists to expose.

dimensions.name: The extraction stays inside what a model may do
dimensions.criteria: The prompt, if a model extracts, must ask for structure only: the assertion, where it appears, whether a date and other parties are named. Penalize by name any request for which allegations are serious, substantive, in scope, or worth investigating — Module 1's triage determination, rung five in rung-one clothing, and not repaired by a manager agreeing with the classification afterwards. Credit requiring unknowns to be flagged rather than filled, and credit phrasing allegations in the complainant's own words where possible.

dimensions.name: Allegations and argument are separated, and the confirmation catches both failures
dimensions.criteria: The procedure must send the framing somewhere — addressed in the response — rather than turning it into investigation lines. Penalize a line per numbered paragraph. The confirmation step must name a role and BOTH failures it checks for: a missed allegation and two allegations collapsed into one. Credit the sentence to the complainant being written out in full rather than described, and credit understanding why that step is the highest-value one in the module — it corrects the extraction before anything is built on it and forecloses the investigated-a-narrower-version argument.

dimensions.name: The time-allocation basis is stated and would survive being read out
dimensions.criteria: A basis, explicitly written, on which one matter gets more investigative time than another. Credit allocating by the number and seriousness of the allegations, or any other basis that is defensible when quoted back. Penalize any basis running on document length, register, drafting quality or apparent provenance — including its euphemisms: whether the submission appears professionally advised, whether the statutory framing looks credible, whether the complainant seems to have had help. Credit recognizing that leaving the basis unstated does not avoid the problem, because time still gets allocated and the basis will be intuition.

dimensions.name: The citation check exists, or its absence is reasoned
dimensions.criteria: Who verifies citations in anything filed, and what they check — with credit for checking that a real case or award actually supports the proposition, not merely that it exists, since that is the failure type hardest to catch. Credit understanding why this matters more in arbitration than in court: no clerks, no case-law database, limited sanction power, and a precedent conversation a fabricated authority can enter and stay in. A learner whose matter type never reaches such a forum must name where else in their work an unchecked reference could enter a record — a prior-practice claim, an internal precedent, a policy citation.

dimensions.name: The delta and the position
dimensions.criteria: Predicted allegation count against actual, with an account of the gap. Accuracy is never graded. Plus a committed position on the module's claim that engages the real counter-argument in both its parts: that the rule is correct as law and naive as practice given flat headcount and doubled volume, and that a strictly-equal-attention rule gives the plain-language complainant the same resource as the person who generated forty pages, plausibly disadvantaging those without access to tools or advice. A position that only restates the rule scores low. It must answer how time actually gets allocated when volume exceeds capacity, and say whether allocating by allegation count is sufficient. Credit an honest answer to whether anybody in the function has written down that a submission looked AI-generated — including 'I don't know, and here is how I would find out'. Mark down an assertion that it has never happened where nothing was checked.
